09 — Architecture

KV-Cache#

Memory OptimizationMathematical 1 min read
◆ The PatternCache once, reuse forever — the key to fast autoregressive generation

// Cache once, reuse forever — the key to fast autoregressive generation

During generation, each new token only needs to compute its own Q, K, V — but it attends to all previous K and V vectors. Without caching, we'd recompute K,V for all prior tokens at every step. The KV-cache stores these, turning generation from O(n²) to O(n) per step.

Step t: K_cache = [K₁, K₂, ..., K_t], V_cache = [V₁, V₂, ..., V_t]
Append new K_t, V_t each step. Only compute attention for the new query against cached K,V.
Memory: 2 · n_layers · seq_len · n_kv_heads · d_k · bytes_per_param
For Llama 2 70B with 4K context in FP16: about 1.3 GB per request with its 8 KV heads, and 10.7 GB if every head had its own.

KV-cache is why batch size during inference is heavily memory-constrained. GQA (fewer KV heads) directly reduces this cost. This is the main motivation behind MQA and GQA research.

KV-cache memory scales linearly with sequence length × batch size. For long contexts (128K+), a single request can consume 40+ GB. This dominates GPU memory during serving.
Interactive — KV-cache growth during generation

Python — KV-cache in generation loop#

Pattern bridge: Caching previously computed keys and values to avoid recomputation. The same memory accumulation that RNN hidden states perform. In markets, support/resistance levels are cached price memories the market doesn’t recompute.
Worked example

Generating 1,000 tokens without a cache recomputes keys and values for the whole prefix at every step: 500× as many projections as with one. The cache has a price: for Llama 3 8B it is 128 KB per token, so a 128k-token context holds 16 GB of cache — as much as the model’s own weights in fp16.

Where it misleads
  • The cache trades compute for memory; on long contexts memory, not arithmetic, limits how many users a GPU can serve.
  • Reusing cache across requests (prefix caching) only works when the prefix is byte-identical.
  • Compressing or evicting cache entries saves memory but can silently drop information the model needed.
In code
T = 1_000                                       # tokens generated
recompute = T * (T + 1) // 2                    # K/V projections without a cache: the whole prefix every step
cached = T                                      # with a cache: one new token per step
layers, kv_heads, d_k, bytes_per = 32, 8, 128, 2   # Llama-3-8B shapes, fp16
per_token_kb = 2 * layers * kv_heads * d_k * bytes_per / 1024
at_128k_gb = per_token_kb * 131_072 / 1024 ** 2
Python, in your browser — edit the code and run it again

Assumes import numpy as np. Configurations named after real models use their published shapes; other numbers are made up or simulated, as the comments say.

The same idea with a library
def generate_with_cache(model, prompt_ids, max_new=50):
    past_kv = None  # will hold cached K,V tensors
    input_ids = prompt_ids

    for _ in range(max_new):
        # Only feed new token(s) — cache handles the rest
        logits, past_kv = model(input_ids, past_key_values=past_kv)
        next_id = logits[:, -1, :].argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        input_ids = next_id  # only the new token
        if next_id.item() == eos_token_id:
            break
    return all_generated_ids

  • W. Kwon et al., “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention”, SOSP, 2023

Check yourself

1. What does the KV cache store?

Show answer

B. Without it, generating token n would mean re-running attention over all n − 1 earlier tokens from scratch.

2. KV cache memory grows with…

Show answer

B. Long contexts and large batches can make the cache larger than the weights themselves.

3. How does grouped-query attention (GQA) shrink the KV cache?

Show answer

A. With 8 KV heads serving 64 query heads, the cache is 8 times smaller than with full multi-head attention.
